bib.title: Machine Learning Engineering in Action, chapter 14: Writing production code

question: What data, monitoring, simplicity and code-architecture practices keep a production ML project alive, seen from an architect's view?
contributions: Three data principles (have the data, check provenance, align on a source of truth) plus fix-at-source
Feature monitoring via stored training statistics (Listing 14.1)
Monitoring across the whole model life cycle
Simplicity ladder from heuristics to custom algorithms
Cargo-cult evaluation flow for new tech

limits: Anecdotal and fictional scenarios; no experiments or measured data.
Numbers in Listing 14.1 come from an unprinted toy series (ORIGINAL_DATA, BOUNDARY_DATA not shown).
Thresholds are ad hoc; author says he does not tune them or use statistical process control.
Tooling references (MLflow tracking, SHAP/LIME, open-source monitoring packages) date from 2022.
Explicitly offers no tool recommendations (section opens by saying tools are fluff).
practices: Before any code, confirm you can get the data needed to answer the problem with an if/else baseline (p.401 tip).
Ask data engineering four questions during EDA: fewest tables, fix priority, access from both training and serving layers, and whether serving queries meet the SLA (p.403).
Record each source's ingestion mechanism, update frequency, SCD type and ownership in a data catalog (p.405-406, Table 14.1).
Check compliance (GDPR, PII, HIPAA), schema change rate, human vs automated source, validation checks and source durability (p.407).
Trust nothing and verify everything about a dataset before modelling (p.408).
Keep one copy of each department's definitions, pick the right SCD type, standardise names, archive unused data and inventory it with ER diagrams or a catalog (p.408-409).
Do not embed data cleansing in ML code; fix issues at the source with examples reported to data engineering (p.410-412, Fig 14.7).
Store training-time feature statistics (mean, median, std, min, max) in a table versioned as SCD type 2 per training run, and run a daily job comparing recent serving values (p.414-415).
Alert via pager or email, not print, and read stats from a table or service such as MLflow tracking (p.416).

Monitor every life-cycle stage: source features, generated features, model metrics per run, prediction distributions, attribution, runtime or response SLA, and feature usefulness via periodic recursive feature elimination (p.418-421, Fig 14.10).
Define the problem with two questions: what should the solution do (prediction type) and what will you do with it (decision) (p.423).
Try heuristics, then linear models or trees, then tree ensembles with SHAP/LIME, and only then deep or custom algorithms, communicating risk at each step (p.425, Fig 14.13).

Create a stubbed project wireframe right after the prototype: ingestion, feature engineering, training and tuning, logging, model registration, inference, tests, decision logic (p.428-429, Fig 14.15).
Mark ingestion, feature engineering, training, logging, testing and decision logic hard requirements; model registration and inference optional depending on serving (p.429, Fig 14.15).
Evaluate new technology: does it solve my problem, can I reproduce it, does it work on my data, do I need it now (p.436, Fig 14.18).
Do not copy big-tech tooling without the same data, infrastructure, staff, use case and budget (p.434).

terms.definition: inexperienced teams latching on to every technology, algorithm, framework and platform from big tech, using complex systems designed for complex problems with no regard to applicability to their own
Overwrite old data; history is dropped
a single copy of each department's definitions that supports its needs, with no _V2 or _V37 copies
a loose and mutable code template of stubbed modules that encapsulates concerns, removable if never populated
